evidence.quote: A recent study by Laube et al. [21] demonstrated that a pseudo-binary diagram (similar to Fig. 1b) for (MoTaTi)92-x-8Cr-Alx can be used to form B2 precipitates within a BCC matrix by tuning alloy composition, providing a strategy for achieving a B2-in-BCC microstructure in RCCAs.
Solution thermodynamics based CALPHAD analysis predicts that such hierarchical structures could be tailored in Nb-Zr, Ta-Zr, and Nb-Ta-Zr systems through optimized two-step aging treatments [23].

While Al-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-V-Zr alloys suffer from B2 phase instability above 1200 °C, recent studies have identified more thermally stable B2 phases.
Frey et al. [24,25] reported B2-HfRu phases with thermal stability up to 1500 °C – 1600 °C in multi-principal element alloys of the HfMoNbTaRuWZr family.
In Ti-Al-X (X = Nb, Mo, Ta) based systems, ternary B2 phases are more stable than the binary Ti-Al, likely due to higher configurational entropy from additional elements.

However, frequent observation of AlxZry type phases (ordered omega type) in the AlMoNbTaTiVZr family suggests their relative stabilization over the multicomponent B2, especially at lower temperatures.
A recent study on Al0.25NbTaTiZr alloy showed a stable BCC + B2 microstructure at 1000 °C, transitioning to a three-phase BCC + B2 + AlxZry microstructure at lower temperatures [87].
Ferritic superalloys, based on Fe-Al-X systems, are optimized for applications below 1000 °C, while RSAs (including RCCAs) are designed for extreme temperatures (1300 °C – 1800 °C).
